Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Caleb Merritt is a 33-year-old married prosecutor who presented for his initial intake describing what he called "a problem I've been managing on my own for too long." His affect was controlled and his language precise — habits, he acknowledged, that had served him well in the courtroom but had made it difficult to admit how significantly his functioning had deteriorated in the months since the attack.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Caleb was attending an evening reception at a federal courthouse, a gathering of legal professionals and local officials that had been organized to mark the close of a high-profile case. He had been working late the night before and arrived at the event already fatigued, accepting a glass of wine he barely touched. He remembers the smell of alcohol on the breath of a colleague who leaned close to speak to him over the noise of the room — and then the explosion. A device concealed in the building's lower level detonated without warning. The blast threw Caleb against a wall. When he recovered enough to move, he found himself in a corridor filled with smoke and the sounds of people who had been badly hurt. Three attendees died. Several others, including a junior attorney he had mentored, sustained serious injuries. Caleb, physically unharmed, spent the next hour helping direct people toward exits, but he had frozen in the first moments — stood still, he says, for what felt like a very long time before he acted — and that initial stillness has become the fixed point around which much of his suffering now orbits.

In the weeks after the attack, Caleb found that his memory of the event resisted the kind of orderly reconstruction he applied to everything else in his professional life. He could not produce a coherent account even for himself — the sequence fractured, certain moments surfacing with a vividness that felt almost physical while others remained opaque. What came to him unbidden was not like ordinary recollection; it carried a quality of immediacy that his memories of his wedding, his childhood, his first courtroom victory did not. When those fragments arrived, they did not feel like the past. He would be at his desk reviewing case files and the corridor would be present again — the heat, the sound, the specific weight of that moment of stillness.

Loud, sudden sounds became intolerable. A car backfiring in the parking garage beneath his office building, a door slammed down the hall — each one arrived in his body before his mind could contextualize it. The smell of alcohol, encountered at obligatory bar association dinners or in the breath of a witness during a deposition, produced the same sudden collapse of distance between then and now. Even exhaustion itself had become a kind of trigger; on nights when he was depleted, the membrane between the present and the event thinned in ways that frightened him.

Caleb had come to believe, with a certainty he found impossible to argue himself out of, that he had failed the people in that room. He was not a first responder, he acknowledged — but he had been there, he had been capable, and he had stood still. He told himself he should have done more to protect others, and that conviction had settled into something that felt less like guilt and more like a permanent verdict. Alongside this ran a quieter, more corrosive suspicion: that the event had been organized by people who had moved through professional circles undetected, and that he had no reliable way of knowing who around him was what they appeared to be. He had grown careful in a way that his wife described as cold, and that he experienced as necessary.

Over the past year, Caleb had declined social invitations, reduced his attendance at evening professional events, and delegated depositions that required him to be in close quarters with witnesses who might have been drinking. His caseload had narrowed without his fully acknowledging why. His wife had told him, quietly and then with more urgency, that she felt she was living with someone who had decided to disappear by degrees. It was that conversation, more than any single symptom, that finally brought him in. What he feared most was that she was right. What he hoped for, though he stated it with characteristic restraint, was some way of putting the event somewhere it could stay.
